opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most deeply ingrained assumptions in our field, and it's very understandable why people make it. We have this algorithm, the genetic algorithm, that was inspired by evolution, and we use it to optimize things. So it's natural to look back at nature and say, "Ah, evolution must be optimizing too, it's optimizing fitness." But when you actually look at what evolution has done, it doesn't really fit that picture very well.

Think about what an optimizer does. It has an objective, and it tries to get as high as possible on that objective. If evolution were optimizing for something like reproductive fitness, you'd have to ask, why didn't it just stop at bacteria? Bacteria are incredibly good at reproducing. There are astronomical numbers of them. By that measure, they're about as fit as anything could be. So why would you ever get trees, or butterflies, or human beings? Most of the complexity on Earth isn't a better solution to the reproduction problem. It's just different.

What evolution looks like to me is much more of a divergent search process. It's this kind of open-ended, non-objective process that keeps generating new niches, new ways of living. Every time something new appears, it creates opportunities for even more new things. A tree makes it possible for something to live in a tree. That's not convergence toward a single peak; it's a proliferation of stepping stones. And the remarkable thing is that it does all this in a single run. It doesn't restart. It just keeps accumulating interesting stuff for billions of years.

And I think the constraint that matters more is something like "survive and reproduce" as a minimal criterion, not as an objective to maximize. You just have to be viable enough to make an offspring. Above that bar, there's enormous freedom. That's very different from saying, "Get the highest score." When you frame it as a minimal criterion plus the accumulation of diversity, a lot of what we see in nature starts to make sense.

The reason this matters for us in AI is that if we have the wrong mental model, we'll build the wrong algorithms. If you think the most creative process in the known universe is an optimizer, you'll keep trying to get creativity out of optimization, and then you'll run into deception, local optima, all those problems, and wonder why. That's a big part of what led to novelty search and to the book with Joel Lehman, "Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned." The punchline is that sometimes the best way to achieve something truly ambitious is to stop aiming at it directly, because the stepping stones that lead there often don't look anything like the destination. Evolution is the best illustration of that principle we have. It's not trying to get anywhere in particular, and that's exactly why it got somewhere so extraordinary.

r002.rationale: It describes “survive and reproduce” as a minimal viability bar rather than an objective to maximize.

r003.rationale: It gives a tree creating opportunities for life in trees, but does not identify innovations such as flight or photosynthesis as side effects of satisfying survival constraints.

r004.rationale: It contrasts optimization toward a single peak with evolution’s divergent search that proliferates new niches and stepping stones.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that it's not entirely wrong. Evolution does have selection, and selection does look like an objective function if you squint. So the optimization framing isn't crazy, it's just that it misses the thing that's actually interesting about evolution, which is what it produced. If you look at the outcome, you have this staggering diversity of forms, everything from bacteria to redwoods to humans writing symphonies. No optimization algorithm I know of behaves like that. Optimization converges. It funnels toward something. Evolution diverges. It keeps opening up new possibilities rather than closing in on a target.

And the thing is, if you ask what the objective of evolution is, people will say survive and reproduce. But bacteria already solved that problem billions of years ago. They're arguably the most successful organisms on the planet by that metric. So if the objective were survive and reproduce, evolution should have stopped there. It should have converged on bacteria and declared victory. The fact that it didn't tells you that something other than optimization is driving the interesting part of the process.

What I think is really going on is closer to what we call novelty search or open-endedness in my field. Evolution is accumulating stepping stones. Every new niche that gets occupied creates opportunities for other niches. The fact that something can fly creates an opportunity for something else to eat the things that fly. It's a divergent, exploratory process, and the reproductive constraint is more like a filter on what's allowed to persist than a goal that's being pursued. The constraint is necessary, but it's not the engine.

And I think this matters practically for machine learning, because when we import the optimization frame uncritically, we end up thinking that if we just define the right objective and climb it hard enough, we'll get something as rich and creative as what nature produced. But nature wasn't climbing anything. The richness came from the lack of a destination, from the search being free to wander and collect interesting things along the way. If you actually want to replicate that kind of creativity, you probably have to let go of the idea that you know where you're going, and that's a very uncomfortable thing to tell an engineer.

astra-6.text:
Well, the key question is: what is evolution optimizing toward? We often say fitness, but that can make it sound as though there’s a fixed objective function, and evolution is steadily finding better solutions to it. In reality, what counts as fit depends on the environment, which includes all the other organisms that are evolving. So the conditions for success are themselves changing.

And there’s no objective in evolution to produce intelligence, or complexity, or human beings. Those are things that emerged along the way. A bacterium isn’t an inferior attempt at being a human. It’s doing perfectly well as a bacterium.

That matters because the optimization framing can obscure the thing we’re actually trying to understand: how does a process keep generating new kinds of things? Natural selection is certainly part of that story. But differential reproduction doesn’t mean the whole process is best understood as progress toward some final target.

I think a more useful picture is an expanding exploration of possibilities. Innovations create opportunities for further innovations, and the stepping stones don’t necessarily resemble what they eventually make possible. If you were selecting organisms millions of years ago based on how human-like they were, you could easily eliminate the very lineages that would eventually lead to us. So evolution illustrates how extraordinary outcomes can arise without those outcomes ever being objectives.

r003.rationale: It discusses innovations and emergent outcomes, but does not identify innovations as side effects of satisfying survival constraints.

r004.rationale: It contrasts evolution with progress toward a final target and describes expanding exploration, but does not make the specified comparison with traditional genetic algorithms.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the problem is that optimization implies you have some objective that you’re trying to achieve, and evolution doesn’t have an objective in that sense. It wasn’t trying to produce human beings. It wasn’t trying to produce intelligence. Those are things that happened along the way, and if we imagine them as the targets, we’re reading the outcome back into the process.

Now, of course, there’s natural selection. Organisms have to survive and reproduce. But that’s a local constraint in an environment that is itself changing, partly because other organisms are evolving. It’s not a fixed objective function that tells you how close you are to some ultimate destination.

The distinction matters because the really interesting thing about evolution is its ability to keep producing new kinds of things. It creates possibilities that didn’t exist before. And those possibilities become stepping stones to further possibilities, even though you couldn’t have recognized their eventual significance when they first appeared.

If you think of evolution primarily as an optimizer, you can miss that creative process. You start asking, ‘How does this get us closer to the goal?’ But often the thing that opens up a whole new direction doesn’t look like progress toward any goal you would have specified in advance. That’s what interests me: how a process can discover extraordinary things without knowing what it’s looking for.
